rows.label: Conditions
rows.text: **Specific Heat Capacity Definition:** $c = H/(m\Delta\theta)$ is the proportionality constant. It is an *intensive* property (independent of mass). The SI unit is J/kg·K. Specific heat varies slightly with temperature for real materials; the constant-$c$ approximation is valid for small $\Delta\theta$.

rows.label: Limitation
rows.text: ❌ Heat and temperature are the same thing. ✅ Temperature is the average molecular kinetic energy (intensive). Heat is the total energy transferred (extensive). A spark at 2000°C has tiny heat content; a bathtub at 40°C has huge heat content.  ·  ❌ A body "contains" heat. ✅ A body contains internal energy (kinetic + potential of its molecules). Heat is the TRANSFER of energy due to temperature difference. Once energy is in the body, it's no longer "heat." Think of it like "payment" - once received, it's no longer a payment; it's just money in your account.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: **Heat is energy in transit:** Heat ($H$) is the thermal energy transferred between systems due to a temperature difference. It is NOT a property of a body - you cannot say "a body contains heat." A body contains internal energy; heat is the transfer of that energy.  ·  **Mass dependency (H ∝ m):** For a given substance and temperature change, the heat required is directly proportional to the mass: $H \propto m$. Doubling the mass doubles the heat needed. This is because more molecules means more total kinetic energy must change.

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: The calorie was originally defined as the heat needed to raise 1 gram of water by 1°C - specifically from 14.5°C to 15.5°C, since water's specific heat varies slightly with temperature. The modern value is $1\text{ cal} = 4.184\text{ J}$ (exact).  ·  Water's anomalously high specific heat ($4200\text{ J/kg·K}$) is due to hydrogen bonding. Breaking these bonds requires extra energy, so more heat goes into the system without raising temperature. This is why oceans moderate Earth's climate.

rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Temperature dependency (H ∝ Δθ):** For a given mass, heat is directly proportional to the temperature change: $H \propto \Delta\theta$, where $\Delta\theta = \theta_f - \theta_i$ (final − initial). Heating water from 20°C to 80°C requires 3× the heat of heating from 20°C to 40°C.  ·  **Combined relation:** Combining both: $H \propto m \cdot \Delta\theta$. Introducing the constant of proportionality - the specific heat capacity ($c$) - gives the fundamental equation: **$H = m \cdot c \cdot \Delta\theta$**  ·  **Sign convention:** When heat is absorbed (temperature rises), $H > 0$ and $\Delta\theta > 0$. When heat is released (temperature falls), $H < 0$ and $\Delta\theta < 0$. The sign tells you the direction of energy flow.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ All materials heat up at the same rate with the same power. ✅ Different materials have different specific heats. 1 kW heats 1 kg of aluminum ($c=900$) much faster than 1 kg of water ($c=4200$). The aluminum's temperature rises ~4.7× faster.  ·  ❌ The formula H = mcΔθ works for phase changes too. ✅ This formula ONLY works when temperature changes WITHOUT a phase change. During melting (ice → water at 0°C) or boiling (water → steam at 100°C), temperature stays constant - you need $H = mL$ instead.  ·  ❌ Specific heat capacity depends on the amount of substance. ✅ Specific heat capacity is an INTENSIVE property - it depends only on the MATERIAL, not the mass. 1 kg of copper has $c = 390\text{ J/kg·K}$, same as 1 g of copper.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ Heat always flows from hot to cold, so a cold object can never lose heat to a hot one. ✅ Heat naturally flows from hot to cold. However, a refrigerator CAN move heat from cold to hot - but only by doing external work (compressor). This doesn't violate the second law.  ·  ❌ If you add heat, temperature always rises. ✅ During a phase change (melting, boiling, sublimation), added heat goes into breaking intermolecular bonds (increasing potential energy), NOT increasing kinetic energy. Temperature stays constant during the transition.  ·  Statement 3: Condition for Heat (H) — Mass and Temperature Dependency to be valid

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Statement 4: Principle governing Heat (H) — Mass and Temperature Dependency  ·  Statement 5: Corollary or consequence of Heat (H) — Mass and Temperature Dependency  ·  How much heat is required to raise the temperature of 2.5 kg of water from 20°C to 80°C? $H = mc\Delta\theta = 2.5 \times 4200 \times 60 = 630{,}000\text{ J} = 630\text{ kJ}$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: A 500 g copper block at 100°C is placed in 200 g of water at 20°C. If no heat is lost, what is the final temperature? Set $m_{Cu}c_{Cu}(100 - T) = m_w c_w(T - 20)$. $0.5 \times 390 \times (100-T) = 0.2 \times 4200 \times (T-20)$. $195(100-T) = 840(T-20)$. $19500 - 195T = 840T - 16800$.…  ·  An electric heater supplies 840 J/s to 2 kg of water. How long to raise the temperature from 25°C to 75°C? $H = mc\Delta\theta = 2 \times 4200 \times 50 = 420{,}000\text{ J}$. Time $t = H/P = 420000/840 = 500\text{ s} \approx 8\text{ min } 20\text{ s}$.  ·  What mass of iron ($c = 450\text{ J/kg·K}$) at 100°C is needed to raise 0.5 kg of water from 15°C to 25°C? $m_{Fe} \times 450 \times (100-25) = 0.5 \times 4200 \times 10$. $m_{Fe} \times 33750 = 21000$. $m_{Fe} = 0.622\text{ kg} = 622\text{ g}$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: A 0.2 kg aluminum calorimeter contains 0.3 kg of water at 20°C. A 0.1 kg copper block at 90°C is dropped in. Find the equilibrium temperature ($c_{Al} = 900$, $c_{Cu} = 390$). Heat gained: $(0.3 \times 4200 + 0.2 \times 900)(T-20) = 1440(T-20)$. Heat lost: $0.1 \times 390 \times (90-T) = 39(90-T)$.…  ·  The concept of "heat" as a form of energy was established by James Prescott Joule in the 1840s. His famous paddle-wheel experiment showed that mechanical work could be converted to heat, establishing the mechanical equivalent of heat: $1\text{ J} \leftrightarrow$ temperature rise.  ·  Joseph Black (1728-1799) was the first to distinguish between "heat" and "temperature." He observed that melting ice absorbs heat without changing temperature - this led to the concept of "latent heat" and the caloric theory of heat.
